641.t: Violin, piano and the circus uncle who steered him to clarinet
641.s: He started on violin and piano, but an uncle who played trombone with a circus told him to take a brass or reed instrument, so he took clarinet lessons from Manuel Rock.
641.q: I had an uncle that used to play with the old Hagenbeck-Wallace circus. The trombone, played trombone. And every year when the circus came to town, I wanted to go with him. And, uh, he

641.t: Choosing the clarinet at about ten
641.s: On his uncle's advice that the circus needs no piano or violin, Joe picks the clarinet over the slide trombone or bass horn.
641.ch: The circus dream and choosing the clarinet
641.q: As soon as my uncle told me that the violin and the piano was out... I was about ten years old then. I guess this violin deal and piano... I was probably 9-1/2 years old or something. Because I know I took up the clarinet about ten, as soon as my uncle told me that. I said, "Well, what should I…

641.t: What Joe wanted from the clarinet; not reading music
641.s: Joe wanted to get out of Baton Rouge and liked the sound; he disliked reading, and the medicine and circus side-show bands needed none.
641.q: I wanted a way to get out of Baton Rouge, for one thing, and I wanted to get on a circus -- because my uncle told me that.

1.t: Drums, uncle Paul's clarinet and lessons with Barney Bigard
1.s: He fooled with drums, tried Paul Barbarin's clarinet, took three or four months of lessons from Barney Bigard at 14 or 15, and nearly became a baker.
1.q: First instrument? I fooled around with the drums. They let me play the drums. I can play a little drums. But the drums, I discussed that from the start. It’s too much [expletive deleted] to haul around. Cymbals, and putting this . . . All drummers had a helper. So my uncle Paul said, “I want you to…

1.t: Clarinet lessons with Barney Bigard and kids practicing everywhere
1.s: Paul sent him to Barney Bigard for clarinet lessons while Don Albert and Herman Henderson also took lessons nearby.
1.ch: Becoming a musician: ukulele, clarinet and the Boozaire Kings
1.q: So he sent me to Barney Bigard. They were working at ...(?)... So I went to see Barney Bigard, and he gave me a little book, and I started figuring out them notes -- and they still all, some of them, the same to me today. So I worked with him for about what...about three months -- when I could…

1.t: Uncle drummers and learning to play
1.s: He first played drums at home with his uncles and was encouraged to learn clarinet; they discuss a relative who played clarinet and died young.
1.q: First instrument, there had a lot of drums around the house. I had three uncles who played drums. Paul Bowman, Lloyd Bowman, and Lucien Bowman. They all played drums. So naturally I'd sit behind Lucien's drums. He'd always play with those 56th Ray Jazz bands, and they'd be mad at us. So I'd sit…

307.t: Buying a five-dollar Albert clarinet and first lessons with Chaligny
307.s: In 1923 he bought a B-flat Albert clarinet with his five-dollar Christmas savings, taught himself hymns, then took lessons from Old Man Chaligny.
307.q: Well, it was, let me see, let me see. It was a little different in a way, but I tell you bands like Rene Punch, Buddy Petit, while they were playing the music almost similar to what we're playing now. Oh yeah. Yes. And sometime it'll be better. Yeah. Because them boys, they just was gifted and they…

307.t: The Albert clarinet, John Lewis's loan, and Gerald Kendrick's band
307.s: He kept the 15-key Albert, borrowed a silver clarinet from John Lewis, rehearsed with Gilbert Young, then joined trumpeter Gerald Kendrick's band that played by ear.
307.q: Kendrick, Gerald Kendrick, uh, trumpet player. Yeah. And, uh, I haven't seen that boy for years now.

307.t: Wellington Knox and the other clarinet students
307.s: His uncle Wellington Knox played in the band; they discuss whether he is related to Emile Knox of the Young Tuxedo band, and boys who gave up lessons.
307.q: Uh, Wellington Knox. Yeah. He gave up the clarinet. And then, quite a few... Is he still living? Yeah, he's still living. Yes. Is he any relation to Mr. Knox who plays drum in the Young Tuxedo band with Casabin? Uh, no. I don't think there's any relation, no. Uh, I don't think there's any relation,…

114.t: Birth, upbringing and getting his first saxophone
114.s: Born in Savannah, raised in Reading and Newark; he loved saxophones in a store window and his uncle bought him a used alto at sixteen.
114.ch: Early life and the Air Force
114.q: Yeah. I told my wife Linda, I told her, “Honey,” I says, “in Newark, New Jersey where I lived, around the corner from where I lived, I lived on West Street, and if you went down the block and turned a corner, that was Springfield Avenue, there was a music store there called Dawn & Kirchner. And…

114.t: Seeing a saxophone in the Newark store window and getting his first horn
114.s: Fascinated by saxophones in a Springfield Avenue window from age 9 or 10, he got an old silver alto at 16 through his uncles.
114.q: As long as I could remember, Lida, I -- my mother said when I was a kid, the washing machine was going a wooka, a wooka, a wooka and I would be in a diaper and I would, like, just dance with it. I guess that was the rhythm. It wasn't music, but it was the rhythm -­

114.t: Buying his first flute in Chicago
114.s: After trying Yusef Lateef's flute in Detroit, he bought a flute from a stranger in Chicago for thirty dollars.
114.q: Oh, I was in Chicago and -- well first of all, before I go there, I was in Detroit one time and we were up at this club where they jammed and Brother Yusef (phonetic sp.) was playing. I forget the name of the club now. And so he was playing flute -­

406.t: From wanting to be a boxer to piano and first seeing a saxophone
406.s: He meant to be a fighter like his boxer father until friend Merle Williams got him to study piano with Josephine Guy. When a community band met, he saw a C melody saxophone and decided that was his instrument.
406.ch: Des Moines childhood and first bands
406.q: Well, I started to play it -- I was playing professionally by then. But my mother got me an alto sax when I was 12. AND to start out. before and it took me about a year, in fact, I had played piano and a week after I got my first saxophone I played my first job the next week.

406.t: Getting his first alto and learning from records instead of lessons
406.s: His mother gave him an alto saxophone for Christmas and sent him to teacher Charles Bushman, whose first lesson was the chromatic scale. He spent the lesson money on movies and learned by copying Coleman Hawkins and others from records.
406.ch: Des Moines childhood and first bands
406.q: Yeah, I just liked the looks of it. I told my mother I wanted a saxophone. She said, 'well, I've spent money with you for piano lessons and you gave it up. Do you think you'll stick with this?' I said, 'Mama, get me a saxophone and I'll learn to play it.' And I wanted a C melody saxophone because,…

406.t: Learning clarinet: Eli Rice's metal clarinet, lessons with Eddie Inge and Joe Burns
406.s: Eli Rice bought him a metal clarinet; Eddie Inge gave him his first lesson in Milwaukee and Joe Burns taught him for almost a year in Chicago.
406.ch: Fletcher Henderson, Ella Fitzgerald and the early 1940s
406.q: When I was talking before and saying I met Eli Rice in Menocwa, Wisconsin, that was 1928. And they took our band to Milwaukee. He asked me did I play the clarinet and I told him yes, but I had never played it before. So he took me to the store and bought me a metal clarinet. And I played it the way…

145.t: Uncle's graduation gift of a clarinet, June 1927
145.s: On his junior high graduation night his uncle gives him a Boehm clarinet and begins daily lessons, so he is first clarinet in high school.
145.ch: Violin, clarinet and the family name
145.q: Well, when I graduated from junior high school in June the 27th, 1927, when I walked down the aisle, I was the last one in the class that walked down because alphabetically, there was nobody in the class with -- that came in my line after the R's, so I was the last one in my class to walk across…

145.t: Uncle Ernest Royal as clarinet teacher
145.s: Ernest was a saxophone and clarinet player who learned the Boehm system and was Royal's only clarinet teacher.
145.ch: Family follow-ups from the first reels
145.q: Primarily, he was a saxophone and clarinet player. He was an excellent clarinet player and he's the one that actually taught me how to play clarinet. He was my only teacher as a clarinet player.

145.t: Starting the saxophone for a supermarket opening
145.s: Royal explains how a school request for a saxophonist led him to claim he played it, and his father showed him the fingering and octave key.
145.q: I'll tell you, my alto saxophone playing started very, very fast and furious and it was strictly not of any choosing of mine at that particular time. I was the concert master in the high school where I was, playing the violin, and I played first clarinet in the band, the military band. So, one day…

9.t: Hearing Johnny Hodges makes him want a saxophone
9.s: His parents were not musical; hearing Hodges at about ten made him want to play saxophone, and he explains why music appealed to Black youth then.
9.ch: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
9.q: : No. No music in the family, except I. And I don't know how it got to me, how I became musically inclined. Well, I know how I become musically inclined. Because I heard Johnny Hodges play, and it was just something about his playing and the tone of his instrument that just appealed to me. And I…

9.t: Meeting Hodges at house rent parties
9.s: He got to know Hodges by following him to totes (rent parties); Hodges would not let him play his horn, and his father could not afford a saxophone.
9.ch: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
9.q: : Yeah, he came home... Then I met him around what they call house rent parties. Up there they have a different name for them; they call them totes. But in New York they called them house rent parties. It was parties in the house. I'd go around to these different little gatherings with other kids…

9.t: The first saxophone, a Pan-American, and slipping grades
9.s: His father bought a second-hand Pan-American alto in his third year of high school; he played free everywhere, his marks fell, and word spread that he sounded like Hodges.
9.ch: Boston childhood, learning music and first gigs
9.q: : I was associated with it. But not for long. Maybe one season or something like that. Because let me see... In my third year in high school, my Daddy decided to buy me a saxophone. Well, I was never a Grade-A student. I would pass, my marks... I was a passable student. But when I got the…

30.t: Learning to read from his uncle and starting on Dodds's E-flat clarinet
30.s: His fiddle-playing uncle taught him to read music; Johnny Dodds lent him a small E-flat clarinet because his fingers were too small, and at 14 he bought his own B-flat clarinet.
30.q: music. Then when I got to read music good, then I got -- in the band I used to play in, the clarinetist was Johnny Dodds. He used to play parades and he used to use an E-flat clarinet, the small one because I was too small to have the B-flat. My fingers wouldn't reach the holes, you know. So he…

30.t: Uncle teaches him to read; Johnny Dodds lends an E-flat clarinet
30.s: His uncle taught him to read music and divide bars, not fingering; Dodds, who played in the uncle's band, lent a little E-flat clarinet that small fingers could manage.
30.q: You see, he taught me how to read the music and the division of the bars and all that. I had a book, you see. And he taught me that. Then when he found out that I could do pretty well like that, they didn't give me a clarinet at all to start with, which I am very happy until this day, you know,…

30.t: Lessons with Lorenzo Tio, reluctantly arranged by his uncle
30.s: Lorenzo Tio, who played with Piron's society band, began teaching him; Lorenzo begged his old uncle to take Bigard on, and the old man liked him and taught him the rest of the way.
30.q: best clarinetists in New Orleans at that time, the great, as far as I'm concerned, Lorenzo Tio, and he played with A. J. Piron's society band at Trenchina's at Spanish Fort.

826.t: Learning violin and clarinet; Frankie Dusen and Pete Lala's band
826.s: Willie E. says he started violin young and clarinet in 1910, and played with Frankie Dusen and in Pete Lala's band.
826.ch: Arrival and the Pete Lala photograph
826.q: I started on violin at five years old. On violin. Yeah, I used to play at the age of 13.

826.t: Self-taught clarinet, favourite clarinettists, brass bands and Kid House
826.s: He says he taught himself clarinet, names clarinettists, played violin at King's Hall, parades with the brass band and with Kid House's band.
826.q: I taught violin. You taught the clarinet by myself. We're probably talking about violin. Yeah, I taught the clarinet by myself.

734.t: Hearing George Baquet with Robichaux and deciding to play clarinet
734.s: Hearing George Baquet on clarinet with Robichaux's band made him decide to learn clarinet; he recalls the band's members and Robichaux's violin.
734.q: Nobody. See? I just picked it up. In fact, sir, when the John Road show came to Thibodeau, George Backe was playing Clownet, you know. George who? Backe.

734.t: Buying the clarinet and Presley Goff's help
734.s: He pawned an alto sax, and Presley Goff taught him the scale on clarinet; he picked it up quickly.
734.q: Well, I... I happened to buy a... And... Uh... I... 된... 된... 된... ! They bought me alto sax when I was playing clarinet. I pawned that and I never could get it out any time before I got it out. I pawned it one carnival. I didn't play, you know. I didn't worry about it. I couldn't get it out. So he…

799.t: Wanting music, quitting school, and buying an Albert-system clarinet
799.s: Youngest of ten, he could not afford lessons, left high school to work, bought a clarinet instead of a trumpet, and still plays the Albert system; born April 14, 1907.
799.q: No, I moved here when I was about six years old, my folks moved here. And I guess from the age of seven I wanted to play music. And being the youngest of ten, by the time it got to me they couldn't afford it. And my sister studied piano and voice for about fourteen years. And I told them I wanted…

799.s: He learned sax and flute by picking them up, doubling for professional jobs; the wooden flute came from Fazola, all before the Depression.
799.q: Oh, you just gradually pick things up, like saxophone. I never did, I just picked one up and fiddled around with it and learned how to play it. And from observation too, you'd watch other people do things. The same way with flute. You'd just pick it up and start noodling around with it and first…

878.s: Larry started Harry on clarinet at about eight, later sent his old thirteen-key Buffet from Chicago, and brother Jimmy helped; Harry taught himself to read a little.
878.q: Then, uh, after he, uh, went up north, he was in Chicago. Of course, I knew quite a bit about the clarinet then, but I didn't own one. How old were you when you started, about? About that time, when he first started me off, I was just a little fellow about eight years old, And he'd teach me a few…

878.t: How Larry got his first clarinet from Freddie Burns
878.s: Larry began at 15 or 16, buying his first clarinet from Freddie Burns, who played with Jimmy and King Watsky; Larry was self-taught.
878.ch: Larry Shields and the Dixieland Band
878.q: Yes, I do remember that. He bought his first clarinet from a fellow by the name of Freddie Burns, who played with my brother Jimmy and played with King Watsky and Buzz Harvey, played bass. And they used to have a little band. They'd go out and play house parties. They all had day jobs, work days,…

84.t: Teaching himself clarinet and leaving for New Orleans in 1918
84.s: He taught himself drums and clarinet, got tips from barber Piku Lazana, and left with Tom Albert in 1918.
84.q: Some of the best made, yeah. How long were you playing drums for? Well, I played drums about three, four years. Then I played a little bass, I played a little guitar, I played a little man on it. And I used to strike a couple of tunes on the piano.

84.s: Inspired by a white barber clarinetist, he got a clarinet and learned it note for note without lessons at 16 or 17.
84.q: It was an apple. And, uh, so he told my daddy to give him the brand new one. Because it was hard to work. He was telling me. It was brand new. And he know more about it than I did. And he swapped it for his own. Well, this one was in perfect condition. I was willing because, uh, that one was hard…

497.t: Father's jam sessions and the classical mouthpiece problem
497.s: He sat in at his father's jam sessions with visiting players but his Selmer C Star sound was too thin until his father gave him a proper mouthpiece; he graduated from Northwestern.
497.q: Well it was kind of funny because I can tell you, he didn’t hear it. But it was kind of interesting, he was conducting these jam sessions in Chicago. And I mean everybody that came through town came there afterwards, from Rahsaan Roland Kirk, Clifford Jordan, Sonny Rollins, you name it. They would…

497.t: Picking up the alto and falling in love with the saxophone
497.s: In a music education class he tried alto, practiced eight to ten hours a day on a borrowed tenor over spring break, and auditioned into the band on sax.
497.q: So after that I thought this, I don’t know if this is really for me. You know? I was beginning to doubt that. And then one day I was in class and I picked up an alto saxophone for studying. Because I was in music education at the time. And we had to study other instruments. And I picked up this…

68.t: Brother's saxophone and first teachers Malone and O'Bannon
68.s: His older brother brings home an alto, and Emmett Malone and Frank O'Bannon start him on the instrument and on transposing.
68.q: : They did. See, all three of them, they were like my father, you know, like my other two brothers were like my father. Of course, they've passed on and the one played saxophone, eight years older -- yeah, the one that was eight years older. He was a saxophone player and actually, he's the cause of…

68.t: Wanting to farm; the saxophone and a white friend teaching him
68.s: He wanted to farm and play trombone, got a saxophone from his brother, and traded jazz for reading lessons with a white friend; Emmet Malone is mentioned.
68.q: Well I really wanted to farm. We had a farm, and I lived on a farm, but my brother, I had two older brothers and one played piano, one played saxophone. But I always wanted to be a trombone player and I used to get the curtains off the wall and slide up and down on the wall. And so I wanted to be a…

824.t: Gallodoro learns clarinet from his father
824.s: Gallodoro describes his clarinetist father teaching him the Albert system clarinet at seven in Alabama, with emphasis on clean playing and counting every note.
824.q: I studied right from the beginning with my father. He was a clarinetist and a very good one also. But he taught me the time and so forth. Incidentally, I forced my father to play the clarinet. Now this is in my documentary that WSKG showed last year twice. And he used to say, “No son, you’re too…

824.t: Gallodoro's early listening: Rudy Wiedoeft and classical study
824.s: Gallodoro recalls hearing Rudy Wiedoeft records in Birmingham, getting his first C melody saxophone at twelve, and later classical study.
824.q: All right. I can remember, I’m born in 1913 and we’ll say 1923, I first heard the famous Rudy Wiedoeft on records. ‘78s. And my father took me to Forbes Music Store in Birmingham, Alabama. I never forgot Forbes, it’s still there. Different owners of course. And naturally I marveled at Rudy…

223.t: Aptitude test and starting clarinet in junior high
223.s: A musical aptitude test leads the band director to hand him a clarinet; he never considers another instrument.
223.q: Grammar schools – I started in Orange. No music that I remember at all. In the first or second grade it‟s pretty rare when you would get music, although I imagine there is some now, because they start the kids pretty early in everything. Junior high school – when we entered, everybody got a musical…

223.t: Kay Kyser movie, high school band and buying a tenor sax
223.s: Seeing Kay Kyser's band inspires him; at Santa Ana High he and a friend buy saxophones and he becomes a tenor player, then starts a stock-arrangement band.
223.q: So that went on for a while. Somewhere along there – this is when I was still in junior high school – I saw a movie featuring Kay Kyser and his College of Musical Knowledge, which was a radio program. They finally put them in a movie. I don‟t know if it was about his program or what, but the band…

142.t: First soprano saxophone at five and first public performance
142.s: His father imported a soprano saxophone in 1953, taught him, and nine months later presented him at a school show with a swing piece among three tunes.
142.q: In 1953 my father imported a soprano [saxophone] from the factory in Paris; probably imported it before because he had to order it. And he taught me how to play it, and nine months later he presented me in public. So, I was five years old when I first picked up an instrument, maybe a little less…

142.t: Clarinet: his father teaches, then Enrique Pablo
142.s: His father taught him clarinet without playing it, until he took Paquito to Enrique Pablo, first clarinet of the Havana Philharmonic, who shaped his technique.
142.q: The saxophone was my first instrument. But then my father had a tremendous time. He learned in those days, he wanted me to be a classical clarinet player. So he learned to play, he bought a clarinet once, imported from the same company. Learn how to play the clarinet. Well, he never majored in…

143.t: Learning clarinet from a book after refusing piano
143.s: Avoiding his mother's piano switch, he took up a clarinet she bought from the Alcoa bandmaster and taught himself from a book.
143.q: Yes, I started playing clarinet. I didn’t want to play piano, because when she’d give lessons she had a switch, and when you’d miss a note she’d hit you across the fingers. So I said, “No-no, not me.” I was a baseball player. So that’s all I did, play baseball. But I used to go around the house…

143.t: Teaching himself clarinet and playing in town
143.s: He taught himself clarinet with his mother's help on notation and played marches for neighborhood kids.
143.q: With the music and the notes. Keys. Signatures on the music and all that. She didn’t know much about the clarinet, but I just read the book and found out about that.

134.t: Buying a C-melody saxophone at a pawn shop
134.s: His father discourages music but he gets a $13 pawn-shop C-melody saxophone, and is then told to try DuSable.
134.q: Yeah, about once every six months he would just shine this piano, because he had a couple tunes that he could play, because he could rag a little bit. That’s ragtime music. He could sit down and really go to town. Anyway, I survived that without being killed. We moved to 5418 South – it was called…

134.t: Finding out his horn is a C-melody; the bass saxophone
134.s: The class laughs when his tenor turns out to be in C; Dyett hands him a bass saxophone while Freeman wants to sound like Lester Young and Hawkins.
134.q: because he’d already put up with Gene Ammons, and Gene Ammons was a little hotshot around the school [?] at the time. Because he mentioned once, “Oh, another little hotshot.” So when I tuned up – which I had never done, because I just started playing with people. I was very gifted – so when this…

491.t: Hearing Lionel Hampton and Arnett Cobb; wanting a saxophone
491.s: After five years of piano, seeing Hampton's band play Flyin' Home made the piano pale; he listened to radio sax solos and his mother, worried about drugs, agreed.
491.q: Yes. Five years. From 9 to 14. That’s when I heard Lionel Hampton and heard Arnett Cobb play Flyin’ Home. The piano paled that afternoon. I’d never heard a big band play live. When that curtain opened – well, they started to play before the curtain

491.t: Mother's surprise gift of a Martin saxophone and first lessons with Ray Ziegler
491.s: His mother bought a new Martin from Wurlitzer's; a neighbor, Tony Mitchell, showed him how to assemble it; teacher Ray Ziegler taught the basics.
491.q: I thought it would never happen, because we were poor. We didn’t have anything. So, if I got one, I thought it would be from the pawn shop, second hand. She never said anything. She went to work that day. I know she didn’t carry any case with her. She carried her lunch like always. I happened to be…

460.t: Tab Smith, the alto saxophone and the Trummy Cain talent show
460.s: Laws saves paper-route money to buy an alto saxophone after hearing Tab Smith's Because of You. He wins a local talent show three times and becomes a teenage sensation.
460.q: Tab Smith, he had this beautiful – then I learned later why he probably had that hit. I listened to this program here in the morning on weekends, Chuck Cecil. He has this radio program. He always plays this stuff from the ’30s, ’40s, ’50s. He calls it, “Music from the Swinging Years.” I learned…

460.t: Getting his first flute for the William Tell Overture
460.s: Sammy Harris wanted a flute solo for the William Tell Overture. A friend gave Laws an old Bettoney flute and he taught himself to play it.
460.ch: Modern Jazz Sextet, the flute and Los Angeles
460.q: Okay. What happened was, the last year of high school, Sammy Harris, the band director I told you about earlier, decided he was going to do the William Tell Overture. The prelude to the William Tell Overture has a big flute solo, but nobody in the band played flute. Just about that time, Sonny…

505.t: Piano lessons, clarinet first, then tenor before the Bar Mitzvah
505.s: His mother made him take piano and clarinet before he got a tenor at about 13; he dislikes the clarinet and they joke about soprano players.
505.q: Yes, because I wanted the saxophone. I was vehement about it. She said, “You must take two years” – my mother. My father, of course – it’s just that my mother was the vocal one. So I always say, my mother. “You got to take two years of piano, because that’s how you’ll know music.” Aw, come on. So I…

505.t: What the Coltrane night meant to a 15-year-old
505.s: The experience showed him music was no hobby: the same tenor he had under his bed could sound like that.
505.q: Eventually. Certainly not that night, although I tell it like it was. Epiphanies don’t happen immediately. They take time to enlarge and magnify and get exaggerated with time, because we exaggerate. But it certainly made me – the main thing is, it made me see, this is not a hobby. What can I say?…

508.t: Getting a clarinet to escape the piano, via Al Hirt and Pee Wee Spitelera
508.s: Bored with piano, he asks for an instrument when Wynton gets a trumpet; his father gets a clarinet from Pee Wee Spitelera, Al Hirt's clarinetist.
508.q: I was always…. We played since we were little. I played piano. I didn’t like the piano very much, so when I was in first grade I had my out I wanted to join the school band, of course, there’s no….

508.t: Loving the clarinet but not practicing; Youth Orchestra and Mr. Demborium
508.s: He took to clarinet but avoided reading, fluffing through orchestra rehearsals until he knew the part, which drove his conductor crazy.
508.q: Yeah. I loved the sound of it. I loved it. I loved it. Still didn’t practice. I didn’t have to. The music we were playing…. We were playing band music, so I guess in a way, I did have an aptitude, but it was incredibly easy music. And then when I was in Youth Orchestra, Mr. Demborium would yell at…

146.t: Buying a clarinet and playing truck houses
146.s: Smith started music around 1923-24, buying a clarinet on credit in the country and then playing blues in truck houses after the move to town.
146.ch: Opening and early years in Dallas
146.q: : Yeah. And then when ...(?)... (?)... out there in the country, and changed the mood in town. We moved here in '23. That white guy who was in the (?). Jones? John(?) Lasiph(?) [PHONETIC] We didn't play nothin' but truck houses. Played blues, nothin' but blues. Truck houses.

146.t: Picking up alto and learning technique from records
146.s: Smith got his first alto from drummer Jesse Dee, names Sauerkraut Collins as the best local altoist, and says he learned fluency from Tommy Dorsey records.
146.ch: Opening and early years in Dallas
146.q: : I picked up alto in '25, it was. Yeah, '25. We got another little band together... No, I was in this three-piece band, the first band, ...(?)...: , a boy named Jesse Dee. He was a drummer, and he had an alto and drums, too. So he didn't like the alto, so he let me have his old alto.

0.t: First clarinet lessons: the high school bandmaster and Buster Bailey
0.s: Started clarinet in the high school band under Professor Tulesty; his distant cousin Buster Bailey, working with Erskine Tate, gave him lessons.
0.q: Because that's the head man of the school, he was named German, descending the wife, the son, and then Buster -- I went with Buster.

0.t: Learning to read clarinet parts; Darnell Howard on three instruments
0.s: Caldwell explains how parts are learned in a school band; Darnell Howard played violin, trumpet and clarinet.
0.ch: Pay, the Fletcher Henderson circle and later life
0.q: Well, he had three trumpets. The man played third trumpet (unintelligible) because (like when could you got we were in high school band, and I started on (unintelligible) beautiful we're going to start you on fourth clarinet clarinet tones, (unintelligible). Well, you got to read. The (are like…

117.t: Skipping a Junior Olympics interview for a C-Melody saxophone
117.s: Winning track events as a boy, Freeman was due to meet an athletic society but stopped at a Wabash Avenue shop window and fell for a C-Melody saxophone; his father was heartbroken.
117.q: And as a matter of fact, Dad got -- since I won this medal, Dad got a letter from some athletic society that seemed to have something to do with a thing called Junior Olympics. I am not quite sure of that now, because I have not kept notes on these things. This is all total recall with me, Helen

117.t: Austin High, the McPartlands and Dave Tough
117.s: At Austin High Freeman meets the McPartland brothers, who persuade his father to buy a saxophone, and he first meets Dave Tough at a Friday social.
117.q: Well, of course, it was not until I was about 15 that I was to meet at Austin High School, I was to meet the McPartland brothers, Jimmy who is still going very strong, of course, married to Marian Mary McPartland, who is by the way coming over here to England and had a marvelous musical career. I…

6.t: Lieutenant Mikell and the 369th Cadet Boys Band
6.s: Procope explains the Mikell name, Mikell's sons, and how Mikell formed the cadet band after Jim Europe's death and offered him a clarinet place; he recalls Buster Bailey as a hero.
6.ch: Discovering Henderson, clarinet and first gigs
6.q: Well, it was '25, then, whatever it was. Whatever it was. So -- well, it ties in about this Mikell, Mikell, yeah, that's what Stanley Dance's name is. We used to call him Michael.

6.t: Getting a clarinet, then a saxophone, and boyhood fellow players
6.s: His father refused a clarinet but his mother arranged one; he played in the Commerce High School orchestra, borrowed a friend's saxophone and got his own alto for Christmas. He names schoolmates Freddy Jenkins, Benny Carter and Farley Jordan.
6.ch: Discovering Henderson, clarinet and first gigs
6.q: Oh, yes. Oh, yes, yes, yes. So I -- so then I went to my father. I said -- now, I've been taking violin lessons now about eight, nine, ten years. Steady, studying the violin, you know. I played in the high school orchestra up on 66th Street, used to be Commerce High School, and we won first prize…

172.t: Clarinet and Jim Humphrey as his only teacher
172.s: He never learned the clarinet; Jim Humphrey was his only teacher and very good to him.
172.q: I did have a clarinet, but I didn't, you know, didn't try to play it. I used to fit a round of wood, I didn't take no lesson.

175.s: He began study with a post-office worker and former trumpeter, learning the Albert-system clarinet with fingering first.
175.q: But it was a funny thing. When I began to study, I studied under an old professor, and that particular time he was in the post office. And his hobby, he'd always loved music, as a matter of fact he played music himself. And I should think there was more or less a sideline for him.

182.t: Professor Ullett, Cantrell and Willie Umford clarinet lessons
182.s: Tom recalls playing with old professor Ullett, drummer Cantrell and his clarinetist son, and taking two clarinet lessons from old man Umford.
182.ch: Early bands and the city, c. 1898-1900s
182.q: Old professor Ullett. He was one of the owners, one of the years used to play violin. I called him Ullett. I played with them. Cantrell used to play drums, a fellow called Cantrell, used to play drums with him. But I know his son.

872.s: Gorman explains how he practiced the saxophone while the others went out, and was soon playing it on the job.
872.q: an extra one you added on to that the fourth one i always see it's made from the carl fisher people so i started fooling around with it and playing it and fooling around saxophon is very very easy you know after you start with it you know i started with it and finally made a skill so his brother…

431.s: Kmen took piano lessons, took up a C-melody saxophone around 1927 and read sheet music.
431.q: I started playing piano very early. I don't remember when. I didn't play it very well, but I played saxophone I guess from the time I was about twelve or so. I should make it 1927 or so. Late 1920s.

922.t: Starting clarinet: solfege with his father, then Lorenzo Tio Jr.
922.s: His father taught solfege first, Manuel Perez was his godfather, and he began clarinet on a C clarinet with young Lorenzo Tio.
922.q: He began with the old method, which often you've heard before, with the solfege. It was singing and for ear training. And then after when he thought I was ready to start on the instrument, then he sent me to Lorenzo Tio Jr.

267.t: Clubs across the river and getting his own clarinet
267.s: After a phone interruption, Ford names the Moulin Rouge, Specs and the Moonlight Inn, and tells how his uncle repaired an old Albert-system clarinet that became his first instrument.
267.q: You want to hear a bit of it? No, wait, no. Not necessarily. Okay, we can go. Because I don't like the sound of my voice. Oh, well, let's see, that's what I, that's what I, that's what I.

619.t: Roofing trade and buying a clarinet to take lessons
619.s: Working as a roofer with his father, he is urged to get a clarinet, buys one and starts fingering lessons, playing in about six months.
619.q: Yeah. And I worked at that so to rent it to you I used to meet him every evening. He said why don't you get you a clarinet? He said you know music already. He said in about six months time you could be making some money. He said I can fix you up in about six months time. Well sure enough I went to…

273.t: Jones's start on clarinet and lessons with Fazola
273.s: After a chat about Snoozer Quinn, Jones says he wasn't into jazz at first. He met Bill Lee on a ship and took up clarinet to play with him, and studied with Irving Fazola in summer 1948.
273.q: I heard quite a bit about him. I didn't know him. He died when I was first getting interested in playing. And everyone was talking about Snooze. I believe he played with White when it was something like that.

277.t: Starting clarinet in Boston, after trombone
277.s: Lovett began clarinet at 15-16 after a few months of trombone, took legitimate lessons, and improvised jazz from the start.
277.q: Bob, when did you start playing clarinet? Probably when I was about 16, maybe 15 years old. That would have been around 1940 or 41. Where were you at the time? At that time I was in Boston, Massachusetts. Do you remember what influenced you to be interested in the clarinet? Yes, I was interested in…

1008.t: Starting on clarinet in his twenties
1008.s: He began at about 22-23, encouraged by Isaiah, buying his first clarinet from Albert Nicholson.
1008.q: Oh, when I started out with music, I was about, I guess about 22, 23 years old. Well, you didn't start when you were a little boy then? No, no. I thought with all those musicians in the family, you might have started doing it. Well, no. I was a man when I started trombone this year. Really? I was…

724.s: After trying harmonica, he buys a used clarinet at about seventeen for nine dollars and needs a new mouthpiece.
724.q: No, I, uh, I tried fooling with harmonica, but that was too hard to fool with, and I was too hard to learn and figuring not to get anything out of it. Yeah. In those days, most everybody played harmonica. You never, boy, you don't own no record or anything. No. And, uh, well I wanted to clarinet,…

800.t: First lessons: trumpet with Chaligny, clarinet with Papa Tio
800.s: His father could not teach him, so he took trumpet lessons from Chaligny at about 15, then switched to clarinet with Papa Tio.
800.q: My dad had started me but he couldn't look like he had no patience to learn to teach me. He sent me to his friend Old Man Shalini. Oh yeah. And I took trumpet lessons. On the trumpet. I took trumpet lessons with Shalini.

191.t: Family music and the first clarinet
191.s: Sisters played piano, an uncle was a country fiddler; Kelly learned from records and a neighbor boy, and bought an Albert System clarinet for $36.
191.q: Well, my two sisters both played piano, but they just studied it and played, you know, very well. All girls at that time were supposed to take piano, so they did. I had one great uncle who was a country fiddler, and then as far as my Irish ancestors were playing, they were musical people too.…

841.t: Schooldays with Bechet's nephew and sneaking his father's clarinet
841.s: Harris recalls going to school with a Bechet nephew and teaching himself on his father's clarinet.
841.q: Sidney Bechet's nephew and I used to go to school together. We used to take up music together. He had a nephew who played banjo and guitar.

636.t: First bands, saxophone then clarinet, jazz as a hobby
636.s: He played with anyone, bought a saxophone at fifteen without lessons, took up clarinet at eighteen, and treated music as a hobby since Australia offered no financial scene.
636.q: Well, I started on, on saxophone, but dropped that, uh, after a few years, uh, and decided the clarinet was, uh, a better instrument, and, uh, the clarinet I was, uh, tried to play.

880.t: Holmes taught Joseph his first notes
880.s: Joseph says that from across the river Holmes came to his home band and taught him clarinet, the first man to teach him a note.
880.q: Sure, I worked with Holmes. Holmes taught me. After I got the saxophone, in fact, I was, I was living on the other side of the river. And Holmes would live on this side of the river. Mmhmm. He used to come over there and we had a little band at home. Mmhmm. He used to come over there, taught me…

306.t: Teaching himself, Floyd Casey's lessons and a homemade first band
306.s: He taught himself clarinet and drums, took lessons from drummer Floyd Casey, and recalls making homemade drums with his brother.
306.q: I picked it up myself. I picked it up myself. I picked it up myself. Now on drum, I picked it up myself, but there's a fellow by the name of Floyd Casey. He came down here with no Faith Marvelous, with Faith Marvel. It was him and Floyd Casey and he was a wonderful drummer too.

886.t: Clarinet lessons and starting with Allen's brass band
886.s: He took lessons from Jim Humphrey, started on B flat and bought an E flat clarinet, and learned funeral playing in old man Allen's brass band, around 1918.
886.q: Yeah. I taught her how to play in Tickets or Lessons. I taught her playing the brass band over the river, old man, Leonard Allen. And the client that I got, he got that pawn shop, he got that pawn shop, probably seven and a half. Then I bought him out, a piece of equipment there.

1052.t: Willie Humphrey, Educational Gateways, and Clyde Kerr Sr. as teachers
1052.s: He identifies Willie Humphrey as his clarinet teacher, won through a Sunday radio show scholarship at about age 12-13, and praises Clyde Kerr Sr. as a major teacher.
1052.q: Willie Humphrey, who's still alive and I think in his 80s now one of the great clarinet players. He and his brother Percy play down at Preservation Hall but Willie Humphrey I met through a scholarship I used to play on the radio every Sunday afternoon when I was in junior high school on a Peter…

198.t: Reel three opening; Bunk Johnson at the Eagle Hall and the first clarinet
198.s: Barnes says no one in his family played, and he first got a clarinet through Bunk after the Eagle Band at Eagle Hall.
198.q: Oh, I was about 17, 18 years old. And I was down there, in front of mine, Johnny Palo, to baseball position. And, uh, got in a crap game down there, which was the crap game out in winter. And I once, they went to the dog and my dad, and I was in the Monday night. And I was in the middle of the…

301.t: Starting on clarinet and sitting in with George Lewis
301.s: Dutre began on clarinet; the first man to let him play was George Lewis, who was with Rena at the time.
301.q: Well, during my time coming up, you would go up to a place and the fellow would say, Oh, boy, go home and let me ask you to kind of think about it. Yeah.

833.t: Taking up the clarinet around fifty; the violin bought for $16 from Fair Charles
833.s: Asked about his clarinet, he says he picked it up himself at about fifty, then recounts buying a big $16 violin in Livonia.
833.ch: Clarinet and lessons with Jim Humphrey
833.q: I was about, let me see, about, about fifty, fifty-someone. About fifty-year-old. Oh, then? Yeah, that's all the time. You weren't a young boy anymore. No. I used to play it too, I'll tell you. But I was playing by, you know. I didn't like it well, you know, playing by, but then I learned it like…

1001.t: Choosing Scott Hamilton over Grover Washington
1001.s: A Rhode Island friend suggested a Scott Hamilton record; Allen wanted that big sound.
1001.q: No it didn’t. Actually when I was first starting to play saxophone, a friend, a saxophone player from Rhode Island where I’m from, suggested I pick up a Scott Hamilton record. So I bought a Scott Hamilton record and I heard the great big sound he had, and I said well that’s what I want to sound…

1013.t: Piano lessons, then taking up saxophone
1013.s: Piano from seven to eleven, quit after a teacher said everything was wrong; at twelve or thirteen an uncle gave him a Selmer and he played a gig the next night.
1013.q: I started playing piano when I was seven and I had lessons ‘til the age of eleven and then I stopped because I changed teacher and the teacher basically said well you’re doing everything incorrectly, you know your posture is wrong, your hand position is wrong, your timing is wrong. We’re going to…

804.t: Trumpet, braces, euphonium, tuba and learning saxophone
804.s: He took up trumpet in high school, switched to euphonium because of braces, then picked up tuba and, while recovering from a hernia, saxophone.
804.q: Yeah. It’s awful really. So I had to go into euphonium, which is a bigger mouthpiece. And for a couple of years I went off the trumpet. And then, about that time, we moved to Australia, and the braces came off. So I started playing the real stuff.

791.t: Joe Viola and getting a soprano saxophone
791.s: Studying with Viola from age 12 or 13 led her to soprano; she still plays the Selmer he picked out.
791.q: Well you know I think I was studying with Joe Viola in Boston, a very fine saxophone teacher. And soprano was a passion of his. So I can remember him pulling it out during lessons and stuff. I started with him when I was about 12 or 13, so I was exposed to it quite young. And when I heard him play…

204.t: First instrument: clarinet, his uncle and the strict teacher
204.s: Brignola taught himself clarinet from his uncle's instrument, took a few lessons from a ruler-wielding Italian teacher who discovered he played by ear, and never studied formally again.
204.q: No, no, my first instrument was clarinet. I had a uncle that lived — my younger uncle who was about ten years older than I am, took clarinet lessons and he was very bad. But he used to leave his clarinet up on the mantelpiece and then he would go out and play. And I used to sit and watch him. So I…

155.t: First awareness of jazz through his roommate; Don and Anne Murray
155.s: His saxophonist roommate introduces jazz; Budd recalls Don Murray, Carson Murray and meeting Anne Murray.
155.q: I suppose in college. My roommate happened to be from Nova Scotia. And he was a saxophone player, but a C melody saxophone. He got me interested in it. He knew players by name, and he worshipped Eddie Miller, even in those days, in the 19 — what was those years — 1931 or 32, and different people.…

803.t: Teaching himself by playing along with Ambassador Satch
803.s: Self-taught, he imitated Edmond Hall on the Louis Armstrong All-Stars record; he discusses taking up piano, saxophone and clarinet, and the clarinet's difficulty.
803.q: I think it was a bit of all of the above. I think the first — because I was very much self- taught when I first discovered jazz. So I did probably what a lot of kids did, there was one record that I’m very grateful to hear because it’s still one of my favorites, it called “Ambassador Satch” and…

668.t: Why clarinet: Artie Shaw, an Albert System horn and teacher Mr. Bruno
668.s: He wanted piano or trumpet, heard Artie Shaw's concerto, and got a $35 C clarinet in Albert System taught by Louis Bruno, switching to Boehm at 13.
668.q: The fact, one I couldn’t figure out how to play a trumpet, and we couldn’t afford a piano. That was my first love was the piano. Second I wanted to learn the trumpet. I didn’t know how you could get all those notes out of just three valves, there was something wrong with that picture. I mean math…

322.s: Paying off the clarinet, getting a school tenor as a sophomore, then a $610 Selmer saxophone; Buffalo musicians' club.
322.q: Well once I paid off my clarinet. You know I was a junior in high school by then you understand, and the clarinet, because I started paying for it in the eighth grade, so in the early part of my — I didn’t start even playing the saxophone until I was a sophomore. I’d been playing on these jobs just…

985.t: Uncle the saxophonist hands him the saxophone
985.s: On the day they moved in, his uncle gave him the saxophone to carry; the uncle then fell ill and never played again, and Evans fell in love with music.
985.ch: The barber shop and Uncle's saxophone
985.q: Um hum. Yeah. But an ironic interesting story. The day we moved to Philadelphia, it was a quick move. So we got to my uncle’s house and we were going to move in with my uncle. He was on the road. And so we were there for two days with him not being there, which was a little weird for me because you…

890.t: Learning clarinet from his father and the violin obbligato
890.s: His father insisted not every son play trumpet; he started Gabriel and cousin Clarence Ford on clarinet after the potato whistle and wrote violin parts for him.
890.q: Well if all of us played trumpet he’d only hire one trumpet player. So he gave me no money. You had to play something to bring some money into the house, to help to support the family. You know what I mean? So he told me and my cousin Clarence Ford, you ever heard of Clarence Ford? Clarence Ford is…

1025.s: A friend in Dalry lent him a clarinet, which began his playing.
1025.q: Clarinet. And that came purely by accident. One of my pals in Dalry, I was in his home one day and they had a tremendous collection of musical instruments all over the place. And he happened to say, “Would you like to borrow a clarinet?” And I said, “Sure, I’d love to.” If he had said trombone I…

941.t: Taking up the sax in high school after harmonica and piano
941.s: Hamilton was already a professional when he started sax in high school; he'd played piano and harmonica first. Music was his one track at sixteen or seventeen.
941.q: I started playing sax in high school. I played other instruments before that but I was already a professional musician when I started on sax so I came to it kind of late.

209.t: Clarinet, then tenor sax after hearing Coleman Hawkins
209.s: He started on piano, then clarinet at ten, and switched to tenor at 15 after hearing Hawkins play Body and Soul. He heard bands on radio remotes and first went on the road at 16.
209.ch: First road band and learning jazz
209.q: Well I started on a little piano, and then I started on the clarinet when I was ten years old, and I played that for about five years. And then I heard Coleman Hawkins play “Body and Soul,” and I thought that’s for me, so I got a tenor saxophone. And I started rather late for a lot of people, I was…

1002.t: Origin of Mama's Licking Stick Clarinet Ensemble
1002.s: As a child of eight, Harrison was punished by his mother with an hour of clarinet practice; Rowe cites Buddy DeFranco's 'agony stick'.
1002.q: My mother, you know every time — when I was eight years old they gave me the clarinet. Eight years old, okay? So for discipline and punishment, if I’d do something wrong instead of giving me a licking, hitting or spanking, “Play your clarinet for an hour today.” You know. And I would hate that. It…

421.t: Switching to the C melody saxophone and early local gigs
421.s: An ad persuades him to buy a Conn C melody sax; he teaches himself, plays by ear in Plainfield bands around 1925-26 and earns money for his father.
421.q: Oh, yeah, that was it. I don’t think the tenor and alto were — well they weren’t publicized. They were trying to push a new thing because the idea of a C melody

594.t: Starting on flugelhorn, then alto at 13
594.s: He began on flugelhorn at 12 because school had no saxophones, then his mother bought an alto at 13.
594.q: Oh, right away, yeah. I mean that was my instrument of choice. I first started playing a flugelhorn, which is like a trumpet, because they had no saxophones available at school. So I played flugelhorn for about a year, pretty close to that. And then my mom bought me an alto at 13. So actually I…

842.t: Father's piano, first saxophone lessons, and Donny James's band
842.s: His father's jazz piano and soprano sax, Depression-era lessons on his father's saxophone, and being recruited at twelve for a Schenectady dance band.
842.q: — in my history. My dad, who actually was a great runner, qualified for the 1928 Olympics, went to Wesleyan, but loved music. And was a pretty decent soprano saxophone player. You can relate to that, had a nice Buescher soprano saxophone which he played at Wesleyan. He graduated in 1928. But then…

656.t: Monk Rowe's introduction; the Benny Goodman Story and a school metal clarinet
656.s: Rowe introduces Militello. In fourth grade he saw the Benny Goodman Story, asked for clarinet lessons, and the school lent him a metal Buescher clarinet.
656.q: Well I’ve always had the talent or the thing about playing, but when I was in fourth grade my mother took me to see the “Benny Goodman Story” and the next day, the next day I went to school and asked could I take clarinet lessons. And we were pretty poor and so the school gave me a clarinet and it…

554.t: Taking up clarinet, alto and flute; first jazz flutist
554.s: Lessons with Louis Arfine, adding flute, and his claim to have brought bebop phrasing to the flute.
554.q: I took up, I guess I was eleven I believe when I had a few clarinet lessons. They used to have a teacher on 48th Street, Louis Arfine. And so I started the clarinet and then came the alto I believe and then you have to play the flute to get into the bands so I started the flute, and it seemed not…

161.t: Lodge band, choosing the clarinet and teacher Mr. List
161.s: A Bronx lodge band recruiter offered him instruments and he chose clarinet inspired by Shaw and Goodman; Mr. List taught him fingerings.
161.ch: New York, the clarinet and first gigs
161.q: So I did that, and I don’t remember particularly performing as performing, but I was taking these lessons, you know, maybe a couple of years of once a week or once every two weeks you know. And I did it and I don’t know what it cost but they had to pay money you know. And my father was not making a…

658.t: Deciding to be a musician and buying a Mark VI tenor
658.s: Seeing Sonny Rollins at the Berkeley Jazz Festival at about 11 made him get a tenor, paid for through gigs and his father's credit union.
658.q: I had already, before I got in my teens, I had already determined that. That was already decided. When I seen Sonny Rollins play a solo saxophone at the Berkeley Jazz Festival when I was about 11, the next day I had to go get a tenor. I guess that would have been the moment. But I wanted to be a…

1012.t: Learning flute and the Illinois doctorate
1012.s: A stepmother's gift of a flute at 14-15, classical lessons in Indianapolis, and the experience of doctoral study at Illinois as the oldest student.
1012.q: Oh yeah, you know it’s interesting that you bring the albums up, because the first album I heard was “Afro Classics” and this is, I think I was 14, 15 years old. My stepmother gave me a flute, I went into a closet and was hyperventilating trying to get a sound out of that thing. And after that I…

416.t: Starting on clarinet in 1927 and first job
416.s: His cousin Frank Reed bought him a ten-dollar clarinet and advised starting on it before sax. He played his first paid job within two weeks, in Brooklyn.
416.q: Yeah. That was my first instrument. My cousin, Frank Reed, who was an excellent musician, was a saxophone player and clarinet. And I sort of looked up to him and he bought me this clarinet for ten dollars you know, in 1927. And it was just wonderful. I started on that and he told me if you want to…

353.t: Singing, piano, saxophone and the flute class with Eric Dolphy
353.s: Singing and instruments came together; she started saxophone at twelve or thirteen, and struggled with flute in college alongside Eric Dolphy.
353.q: It was all going on at the same time. It was all going on at the same time. Maybe singing first, because I didn’t start the saxophone until I was about twelve, thirteen. But I had piano and I regret to this day that I didn’t keep it. I can play just to teach myself songs or things, but I didn’t…

994.t: Saxophone first, then stumbling on the steel pan at Appalachian State
994.s: He doubts he would still be in music had he stayed on sax; a friend took him to the panyard at college and the pan felt natural after sax and drumline.
994.q: Well that’s deep because with every little thing that happens in life we never know which path takes us down so there’s a chance that if I still played the saxophone, which was my first instrument, maybe I wouldn’t be doing music. There’s no telling, you know? So it’s hard to even make a parallel…

410.t: Meeting Goodman, Ramapo workshop and teaching himself tenor sax
410.s: Getting Goodman's autograph, the Ramapo jazz workshop faculty, and self-teaching tenor from a Lester Young solo.
410.q: know I said oh my God, you know. He went, “Well would you like to come with me.” “Would I like to come with you?” But then how am I going to — my father is going to have to drive back and leave me for three or four hours and then either go back to Fairlawn or go sit somewhere, and I went with Teddy…

423.t: How Ed started drums; Joe Rider and Houston Person's sax
423.s: Ed was lukewarm on piano; his scoutmaster Joe Rider taught drums, and he compares his story to Houston Person being given a tenor sax.
423.q: No I didn’t love the piano. I didn’t hate it but I didn’t love it. Well I don’t know because I had one other little connection to the drums. I was a Boy Scout and my scoutmaster, who I adored, I thought was a wonderful guy named Joe Rider. Joe taught drums, and he wasn’t a sit down drum set player,…

459.t: Eastman, jazz there, and first record date with Morton Gould
459.s: Eastman humbled him; jazz was unofficial; he played alto sax on Gould's Latin American Symphonette in 1951.
459.q: Then I found out there’s millions of good players in this country. But I did very well at Eastman, I was very fortunate.

361.t: Rheumatic fever, clarinet, sax and then piano
361.s: Illness kept him home, so he got clarinet and saxophone lessons and then piano.
361.q: Yeah. I played clarinet and alto saxophone, which I play today, I play alto saxophone now. But how that ever happened was I was more involved as a kid with sports, like a lot of kids. I was always running around playing football and baseball. And lo and behold I got rheumatic fever, and I had like…

934.t: Starting on flute in the Philadelphia school system
934.s: He wanted clarinet but was lent a flute, got a poor teacher, then at 15 heard jazz and later got a saxophone.
934.q: Well what happened I mean I started with my first instrument actually when I was a kid in the Philadelphia school system. They would lend you instruments. They had a program and they could provide some kind of a teacher. And I wanted to play, I thought it would be nice to play something and I…

701.t: Getting bit by the jazz bug at Tottenville High School
701.s: A stage band concert in tenth grade on Staten Island inspires Thomas and his friend Mason Ashe; he borrows an alto sax and works his way into the stage band by senior year.
701.q: Yes, big time. Big time. Even before Hamilton, in high school is where I got bit by the jazz bug. And that happened, I actually know the moment. I know the moment it happened. It was at a Tottenville High School stage band concert. Mason Ashe, also a graduate of Hamilton class of ’85, he and I went…

1044.t: Starting on clarinet and saxophone, father's tenor
1044.s: Watson began at ten; his father, an FAA inspector who tuned pianos and played tenor, kept music in the house. He started clarinet and piano, moved to tenor then alto around 1970, and first played in church.
1044.q: Well I started in music when I was ten years old. My father, he made a living flying airplanes and worked for the FAA. In fact he was one of the first blacks to become an inspector, the ones that go in and get the black box when a plane crashes in the country. But the way he worked his way through…

552.t: Why the saxophone: Swiss Movement and Eddie Harris
552.s: He wanted to be a drummer but switched after hearing Les McCann and Eddie Harris and Cannonball records.
552.q: Yeah. Formally anyway. I really wanted to be a drummer, before the age of twelve. But I think what changed me to saxophone was hearing the record “Swiss Movement,” Les McCann and Eddie Harris. Because that was a big hit around 1969, 1970, and that was one of the records my father had and I…

449.s: Records by Miles, Clifford Brown, Coltrane and Rollins led him to ask LeBlanc for a tenor.
449.q: You know I always loved it because I was into Miles and Clifford Brown and they had — Clifford had Sonny Rollins and Miles had Coltrane and Hank Mobley. So I always was attracted to it from the trumpet records I had. So I was endorsing trumpets for LeBlanc. I was 13 years old, and I asked Vito…

85.t: Out of school, the trumpet returned, a C melody saxophone from Harold Proctor
85.s: After leaving school he returned the trumpet he had bought, took a C melody saxophone and a few lessons from neighbor Harold Proctor.
85.q: No, I think, as a matter of fact, my mother tried to get me to go to another school further uptown, and I just wouldn’t go to school. No, I was never picked up as a runaway,

368.t: First clarinet teacher Happy Cotrill and the reunion decades later
368.s: Virgil 'Happy' Cotrill taught him clarinet first, and they met again after sixty years.
368.q: …I was at first. But then an itinerant musician, Virgil Cotrill, we used to call him “Happy.” “Happy Cotrill” was living in the neighborhood and he was my first clarinet teacher, but he said I should play clarinet first and not saxophone because if you play clarinet first the sax will come easier.…

503.t: Billy goes to the army and Burrell wants a saxophone
503.s: At twelve he decides to play music, drawn to tenor players like Hawkins and Young, but the family had no money and metal was rationed.
503.q: So, Billy went off. Donald was in the hospital, he had a back problem which kept him in the hospital for a couple of years. And so, I just being a kid with baseball and all the other things that kids do. All of a sudden at about age twelve, maybe going on thirteen, I got this real interest in…

133.t: James Clay, clarinet by ear and band director J.K. Miller at Lincoln High
133.s: He recalls James Clay in the high school band and J.K. Miller letting him play clarinet by ear, mentions studying bass later at Denver, and notes touring Japan with Clay and Fathead Newman as Texas Tenors.
133.ch: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
133.q: Yeah, well, uh, he sat behind me in the uh high school band. I was struggling. Well, I was playing the clarinet really by ear. I, I, the uh written note gave me enough, not only gave me problems on the piano – I mean, sight reading, you know – I would have to work on it, then I could play it, you…

105.s: Hamilton remembers Dexter Gordon as a tall kid called Big Stoop from a wealthy doctor's family, who played clarinet then.
105.q: His father was a doctor, you know, and I think he grew up on the west side or something like -- you know, but he was cool.

107.t: Taking up clarinet after a Wurlitzer ad
107.s: A friend's remark about a newspaper ad led Foster to ask for a clarinet, bought for $75-100 and paid off through lessons.
107.q: That’s an interesting story I think. I have a childhood friend whose name is Morrison Bishop. We’re the same age. We lived close to each other. We were looking at a daily newspaper one day, and we saw an ad in the paper by Wurlitzer Music Store for music lessons. There was a picture of a clarinet…

372.t: Benny Goodman, the clarinet, Lou Honig and moving to saxophone
372.s: Goodman inspired him to take up clarinet at about eleven; he describes a coupon-book lesson deal with teacher Lou Honig and getting tenor then alto.
372.q: Well, I was very moved by his band and his clarinet playing, more so than Artie Shaw . . . that was the reason I asked for a clarinet, because of his inspiration.

408.t: Inheriting his uncle's saxophone and the first lesson with Harvey LaRose
408.s: At twelve he finds the dead uncle's saxophone, intends to melt it, and ends up taking lessons from Harvey LaRose.
408.q: But he had a saxophone and at the time he was very sick, in fact he was dying of cancer, and they lived downstairs from where I lived with my mom and dad he lived downstairs with my grandmother and uh my mother’s sister, who he was the husband of my mother’s sister, Phyllis, and uh I discovered…

953.t: Louis Jordan and getting his first alto saxophone
953.s: Louis Jordan records and a photo outside a club made him want the saxophone; his mother got him a second-hand alto at seven or eight.
953.q: Well, I uh that I was almost destined, you know? I, uh...my first really hero was Louis Jordan, the alto saxophonist, and he played tenor, also. But um, he drew me because we had his records at home, and uh...it’s sort of a weird circle the way these things happen. I used to go to school,…

63.t: Why he took up the saxophone: vaudeville, New Haven, anti-Semitism
63.s: Shaw refers to his autobiography, says he grew up in New Haven facing anti-Semitism, and chose the saxophone as his way out after seeing a vaudeville player.
63.ch: Early years: Cleveland, Aaronson, New York
63.q: Well, quickly, I got hold of a saxophone and learned to play saxophone. I’m the only world-class clarinet player who started on saxophone.

553.t: The Arcade Theater and buying an alto saxophone
553.s: At twelve he hears stage-show bands, wants trumpet, settles on saxophone and buys an alto at 18, starting at Sydney D. Miller High School.
553.q: At home and in the church. Also, in the environment, the neighborhood. Um, for example, when I was twelve...uh downstairs under the place I lived there was a theater called the Arcade [pronounced: arcade-e] Theater, in Detroit, Michigan, and I would sit there in the front row. They had stage, what…

65.t: Meeting Mario Bauza and his musical training
65.s: Machito met Mario at Pobolote through his sister Estela; Mario was a trained clarinetist taught by Hugo Cien and Arturo Andrade.
65.ch: Mario Bauza and the Cuban sextets
65.q: I was about sixteen. Estela was about twelve and Mario was about fourteen. I am older than Mario two years; but Mario was an accomplished musician. He was playing with the Philharmonic.

89.t: Summer 1916 with the circus and teaching himself clarinet
89.s: After four years of piano he took up clarinet at fourteen, self-taught with occasional tips from his uncle.
89.q: with the circus and I did a season with the circus sitting beside my uncle. He played E-flat clarinet and I played B flat clarinet. Incidentally, we didn't bring in the time that I started studying clarinet. Four years of piano and then I had -- from 14 on I started studying clarinet.

90.t: Lessons with Arthur Horn and the first alto
90.s: A boarder, Arthur Horn, taught him for 35 cents a lesson paid in laundry; an uncle's C.G. Conn alto was acquired the same way.
90.q: Yes, and I'd like to get back to the very beginning of my association with the instrument. There was a saxophone player living at our house, renting a room. You know, in ...(?)... plenty of rooms, and two beds in one room and all that type of thing. And he lived there with us... So my mother…

452.t: Getting the tenor saxophone chair in the school stage band
452.s: When the stage band's tenor player falls ill, Cobb is pulled out of Latin class to rehearse and takes over the tenor, which he has played ever since.
452.q: Finally, one day in Phyllis Wheatley High School where I attended and graduated in 1935, my first class to me was rotten and I had a teacher that was so firm -- she was a Christian Scientist. She didn't believe in you getting sick or nothing. And the tenor saxophone player took sick and we were…

232.t: Earl Bostic, Tulsa High School and the broken clarinet
232.s: Band director William Jett gives young Earl Bostic a clarinet, which Bostic's junk-dealer father breaks; Fields also notes Bostic subbing for Luther West.
232.ch: Building the band: Dave Duncan, Denver and Rene Hall
232.q: So I went on back then, when we did go back in Tulsa, we played those dates-- what's his name--Dorsey--had several dates and we played around and went back and Spurgeon was still going to school down in Xavier and I never would encourage him to stop school and I think Bostic had Scott around, Earl…

92.s: His mother chose clarinet and a Japanese teacher; he hated it at about ten and was drawn to strings.
92.ch: Looking back: rock, blues, childhood and guitar innovators
92.q: Well, I don't know, I didn't choose the clarinet. My mother chose the clarinet before me. And she got this Japanese teacher for me, and I don't think we could communicate too well. This is another reason I think I didn't like the instrument. And I always was drawn to strings, you know, so --

235.t: Father's Albert System clarinet and learning to read
235.s: He picked up his father's Albert system clarinet, switched to Boehm system, and relied on piano training for reading.
235.q: Yeah. Yeah, well my father had one, an old Albert System around the house. He started me on the piano at nine, you see, and then he had an old Albert System clarinet around the house...he was very sophisticated, you know, he just laid it there, you know, so I picked it up and I started playin' it,…

169.t: Boley training school: the trumpet he wanted, the clarinet he got
169.s: Bandmaster George Buford taught him fingering but put him on clarinet; he learned it and became the better of two clarinettists before leaving Boley.
169.ch: Childhood and first music in Oklahoma
169.q: : Yeah. Well, I had heard Louis Armstrong, you know, and I figured, 'Well, hell, that's what I want to play. I want to be like Pops,' you know. But when they got the instruments for the school band, the cat, George Buford, who was my music teacher, he had taught me the scale on the trumpet...

389.t: Violin traded for a C-melody saxophone and lessons
389.s: He gave up the violin for a Wurlitzer C-melody saxophone, took lessons from a Bohemian clarinetist and was soon invited to play paid jobs.
389.q: But I did want to get an instrument early. I wanted to take lessons. First of all, they got me a fiddle, got me a violin. You know a violin, if you wanted to get any sounds out of it, it was going to take your three or four years before you could make the sounds, and it was nothing more -- except…

124.t: High school band, buying a tenor saxophone
124.s: McRae joins the high school band, works in Dr. Miller's drugstore, buys a saxophone from a pawnshop after hearing a tenor solo with Paul Whiteman.
124.ch: Philadelphia and the McRae Brothers Band, 1908-1929
124.q: I couldn't remember. That used to bug me a lot. I always wanted to know who some of those people were, but I didn't bother about it because eventually when I got into high school, I got into the band -- played in the high school band.

7.t: Teaching himself saxophone and gigging in Topeka
7.s: Hearing Alphonso Trent's band in Oklahoma, he learns C-melody sax from a schoolmate, buys his first horn from Jenkins, and by the third year plays a weekly gig in Topeka.
7.q: And I had... See, I didn't have no idea I had this talent for music. But in Oklahoma, in them early days, we heard so many good bands nad good Blues players, and guys played piano. Alphonso Trent's band used to come through there, and he had a great band. And I heard this, and that music was kind…
